I'm researching how the LEGACY WriteGrader system integrated with Canvas LMS, specifically two things. Read-only; do NOT edit. Search these repos:
- /Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/writegrader-backend (Express/Lambda, this is the main legacy backend)
- /Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/writegrader-kronos (Zig newer API)
- /Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/atlas (shared schemas, packages/core/src/models)
- /Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/writegrader-frontend

QUESTION 1 — LTI: Does legacy WriteGrader implement LTI (Learning Tools Interoperability) at all? Grep for: lti, LTI, lti_client_id, client_assertion, id_token, deep_link, deeplink, nrps, "names and roles", ags, "assignment and grade", oidc, jwks, "/lti/", platform, deployment_id, "1.3", launch. If LTI exists, describe: which version (1.1 vs 1.3), what placements (course nav, assignment, deep linking), whether it does NRPS (roster) and AGS (grade passback), and the route paths + key files. If LTI does NOT exist, say so clearly.

QUESTION 2 — Enterprise/institution-wide Canvas token: How does legacy WriteGrader authenticate to Canvas? I specifically want to know if there's an ENTERPRISE-WIDE / INSTITUTION-WIDE Canvas API token or service account, as opposed to per-instructor personal tokens. Grep for: canvas, GROUP.canvas, group.canvas, canvasToken, canvas_token, accessToken, apiToken, "developer key", clientId, client_secret, refreshToken, org-login, "/canvas", verify-user, instructure, subaccount, "account_id", masquerade, "as_user_id", admin token. 

Look especially at:
- atlas group/school schema's `canvas` field shape (what does GROUP.canvas store? a token? client creds? a domain/account id?)
- writegrader-backend routes/canvas.ts and any canvas controller/service
- How a Canvas API call picks its credentials: does it use a single org-level token for all courses in a group, or each teacher's own token?

Report concretely: the Canvas auth model (per-user vs institution-wide token vs OAuth dev key vs LTI), the schema field names that store Canvas credentials at the GROUP/institution level, the file paths, and how API calls select credentials. Distinguish clearly between (a) a stored institution-wide API token/service account, (b) an OAuth client_id/secret developer key that still mints per-user tokens, and (c) LTI. I need to know exactly which of these legacy uses. Don't dump whole files; give shapes, field names, and mechanics.

-- Institutional Canvas OAuth — per-school developer-key config.
--
-- First slice of "institution setup": lets a school register one Canvas
-- Developer Key (client_id/secret/domain) so its teachers SSO in via OAuth
-- instead of each pasting a personal API token. Per-teacher OAuth *tokens*
-- already have a home (lms_connections: access_token/refresh_token/scope/
-- token_expires_at); this table holds the *app* credentials.
--
-- Secret handling mirrors lms_connections.access_token (see 0100_canvas.sql):
-- the client_secret is stored plaintext but the table denies all access to
-- authenticated/anon — only the service-role client (server-side, behind the
-- global-admin gate) can read or write it. We do NOT put this on
-- schools.canvas_config: that column is granted SELECT to authenticated AND
-- anon (RLS-gated by is_school_member), so any school member could read a
-- secret stored there.
--
-- Future: wrap client_secret in a pgsodium secret column for at-rest
-- encryption (same TODO as lms_connections.access_token).

create table if not exists public.lms_institution_configs (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  school_id uuid not null references public.schools (id) on delete cascade,
  service text not null default 'canvas',
  domain text not null,
  client_id text not null,
  client_secret text not null,
  enabled boolean not null default false,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  updated_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  -- One config per (school, service, domain). domain lets a school that
  -- spans two Canvas hosts hold both.
  unique (school_id, service, domain)
);

comment on table public.lms_institution_configs is
  'Per-school LMS OAuth app credentials (Canvas Developer Key). Service-role only; never exposed to authenticated/anon.';
comment on column public.lms_institution_configs.client_secret is
  'Canvas Developer Key secret. Service-role read only. TODO: pgsodium at-rest encryption.';
comment on column public.lms_institution_configs.enabled is
  'When true, teachers in this school see "Connect with {school} Canvas" (OAuth) instead of the personal-token form.';

create index if not exists lms_institution_configs_school_idx
  on public.lms_institution_configs (school_id);

-- RLS: deny everything to authenticated/anon. No policies are created, so all
-- access from those roles is denied. The service-role client bypasses RLS and
-- is the only path (used by the global-admin-gated admin UI and the OAuth
-- routes). Revoke the broad default grants Supabase hands to authenticated/anon
-- so the credentials are unreadable even if a future policy is added by mistake.
alter table public.lms_institution_configs enable row level security;
revoke all on public.lms_institution_configs from authenticated, anon;

Clear picture on the current lawgrader side already. One correction is forming that I want to verify against legacy before I state it. Let me wait for the legacy agent, since both your questions hinge on what legacy actually does.

Here's what I can already confirm on the **current** lawgrader side, because it bears on your question 2: what was recently built (`lms_institution_configs`, migration 0219) is a per-school **OAuth Developer Key** (client_id + client_secret + domain). That is *not* an enterprise-wide token. It's an OAuth *app* credential that still mints a separate token *per teacher* through the OAuth flow (those land in `lms_connections` as `scope='oauth'`). So the recent buildout is option 2 (institution-sponsored per-teacher OAuth), not a single shared institution token.

But you're onto something real: there's a vestigial `schools.canvas_config` (jsonb) and `schools.lti_client_id` column in the schema, both mirrored from legacy, both **completely unused** in app code today. `canvas_config` is the plausible home for an enterprise-wide token. Let me confirm what legacy stores there and whether it's a true god-token model before I lay out the full option space.

<result>## Report: Legacy WriteGrader Canvas LMS Integration

Based on comprehensive code search across all four repositories, here are my findings:

---

### QUESTION 1: LTI Implementation

**Status: CUSTOM/DEPRECATED LTI (NOT standard 1.1 or 1.3)**

Legacy WriteGrader does implement LTI, but it's a **custom, deprecated implementation** rather than standard LTI 1.1 or 1.3. No standard LTI libraries or full spec features are present.

**Key Details:**

- **Route**: `GET /lti-launch` 
- **File**: `/Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/writegrader-backend/lambda/src/routes/loginRoutes.ts` (lines 111-211)
- **Auth Method**: Custom LTIK-AUTH-V2 header authentication
  - Takes `ltik` query parameter
  - Uses `LTI_KEY` environment variable (defined in `.env` as UUID: `9db92828-15d3-4f99-8358-c8238e6ed952`)
  - Constructs header: `LTIK-AUTH-V2 ${API_KEY}:${ltik}`
  
- **External Service**: Calls `https://lti.writegrader.com/api/idtoken` (not standard Canvas OAuth)
  - Returns: `user`, `platform`, `launch`, `services` objects
  - Matches group via `lmsInfo.clientId` against GROUP's `ltiClientId` field

- **Schema Field**: `ltiClientId` in GROUP schema (`atlas/packages/core/src/models/schemas/group.ts`, line 29)
  - Fallback default: `"NOT_A_REAL_KEY"` (suggesting placeholder status)

- **Role-Based Routing**:
  - Instructors → `https://writegrader.com/#/login/{signupCode}?group={groupName}`
  - Students → `https://student.writegrader.com/`

- **Missing Features** (no trace of):
  - NRPS (Names and Roles Provisioning Service)
  - AGS (Assignment and Grade Service)
  - Deep linking
  - Standard OIDC/JWKS validation
  - LTI 1.3 placements (course navigation, assignments)

**Conclusion**: This is a minimal custom LTI bridge (likely early experiment) marked deprecated in code. Does NOT implement standard LTI 1.1 or 1.3 spec.

---

### QUESTION 2: Canvas Authentication Model

**Status: HYBRID - Institution-wide OAuth2 + Optional Per-User Tokens**

The system uses **both** an institution-level Canvas developer key AND optional per-instructor personal tokens, with a clear priority order.

#### A. Institution-Level Canvas OAuth2 Developer Key

**Stored In**: GROUP schema (DynamoDB record)

**Fields** (`canvas` object in GROUP):
```typescript
canvas: {
  clientId: string,        // Canvas OAuth client ID
  clientSecret: string,    // Canvas OAuth secret
  domain: string,          // Canvas instance domain (e.g., "canvas.test.edu")
  scope?: string          // Optional OAuth scopes
}
```

**File**: `/Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/atlas/packages/core/src/models/schemas/group.ts` (lines 8-13)

**Used For**:
- OAuth2 authorization code exchange → access token + refresh token
- Token refresh when expired (lines 81-86, canvas.ts)
- Falls back if no per-user token available

#### B. Per-User Personal Canvas API Tokens

**Storage**: 
- **Cookie**: `userCanvas` (JWT-encrypted)
- **DynamoDB**: `pk: "UCT#<email>"`, `sk: "UCT#<email>"`, `DATATYPE: "USER_CANVAS_TOKEN"`
- **File location**: `/Users/murff/Documents/write-grader/writegrader-backend/lambda/src/routes/canvas.ts` (lines 270-286, 651-686)

**Encryption**:
```typescript
encrypted_token = encrypt(token, req.user.createdAt + JWT_SECRET)
```

**Purpose**: Allow instructors to use their own Canvas API token instead of institution OAuth

#### C. How Credentials Are Selected (Priority Order)

**canvasMiddleware logic** (canvas.ts, lines 40-115):

```
IF req.cookies.userCanvas exists:
  ├─ Decrypt: decrypt(req.canvas.encrypted_token, user.createdAt + JWT_SECRET)
  └─ USE PERSONAL TOKEN → req.canvas.access_token

ELSE IF req.cookies.canvas + req.cookies.canvasAccess exist:
  ├─ Check if expired
  └─ IF expired:
     ├─ GET group.canvas.clientSecret + group.canvas.clientId
     ├─ Call refreshAccessToken() → new access_token
     └─ Update canvasAccess cookie
  
  └─ USE INSTITUTION TOKEN → req.canvas.access_token

ELSE:
  └─ Return 404 Unauthorized
```

#### D. Canvas Routes & Token Usage

All routes protected by `canvasMiddleware`, which populates `req.canvas.access_token`:

| Route | Purpose | Auth |
|-------|---------|------|
| `POST /lms/canvas/org-login` | Return institution Canvas config for OAuth setup | None (query `institutionName`) |
| `POST /lms/canvas/login` | Exchange OAuth code for tokens | Institution clientSecret |
| `POST /lms/canvas/user-token` | Upload personal Canvas token | User token required |
| `GET /lms/canvas/refresh-token` | Refresh canvas token | Auth required |
| `POST /lms/canvas/comment` | Post grade/comment to Canvas | Bearer token from req.canvas |
| `GET /lms/canvas/courses` | List courses | Bearer token |
| `GET /lms/canvas/courses/:courseId/assignments` | List assignments | Bearer token |
| `GET /lms/canvas/courses/:cid/assignments/:aid/submissions` | List submissions | Bearer token |

#### E. Security Measures

- **Institution secrets never exposed**: `delete Item.canvas.clientSecret` before returning group info (`org-login` route, line 302)
- **Per-user tokens encrypted** at rest and in cookies
- **Explicit cleanup**: Routes to delete saved user tokens (`DELETE /lms/canvas/save-token`)

---

### Summary Table

| Aspect | Finding |
|--------|---------|
| **LTI Support** | Custom deprecated implementation; NOT LTI 1.1/1.3 compliant |
| **LTI Version** | N/A - uses proprietary LTIK-AUTH-V2 against external service |
| **LTI Placements** | Role-based redirect only; no standard placements |
| **NRPS/AGS** | NOT implemented |
| **Canvas Auth Type** | **Hybrid**: Institution OAuth2 dev key + optional per-user personal tokens |
| **Institution-Level Storage** | GROUP.canvas object (clientId, clientSecret, domain) |
| **Per-User Storage** | DynamoDB (UCT# prefix) + encrypted cookies |
| **Token Selection** | Per-user token preferred; falls back to institution token |
| **Grade Passback** | Manual API calls via `/lms/canvas/comment` (NOT standard AGS) |
| **Key Files** | `/writegrader-backend/lambda/src/routes/canvas.ts`, `/atlas/packages/core/src/models/schemas/group.ts`, `/writegrader-backend/lambda/src/routes/loginRoutes.ts` |

---

The legacy system is **neither pure LTI nor pure per-user OAuth**—it's a **pragmatic hybrid** where institutions configure Canvas OAuth credentials once, but instructors can optionally override with personal tokens.</result>

Both answers are in, and they sharpen your question 2 in a way worth being precise about. Let me correct one thing in your mental model, because the distinction matters operationally.

## Q1: Does legacy do real LTI? No.

Legacy has a **fake/deprecated LTI bridge**, not standard LTI. It's a custom `LTIK-AUTH-V2` scheme that calls an external `lti.writegrader.com/api/idtoken` service, matches a group by `ltiClientId`, and then just **redirects** the user to the right WriteGrader URL based on role. No NRPS, no AGS, no deep linking, no OIDC/JWKS, no real placements. The `ltiClientId` field even defaults to `"NOT_A_REAL_KEY"`. So legacy effectively **punted on LTI** and went the OAuth-dev-key route instead. The `schools.lti_client_id` column in your current schema is a dead mirror of that abandoned experiment. Bottom line: nobody has built real LTI. Greenfield if you want it.

## Q2: The "enterprise-wide token" — precise version

Here's the correction. What legacy actually stores at the institution level (`GROUP.canvas`) is `{ clientId, clientSecret, domain, scope }`. That is an **OAuth Developer Key**, not a stored access token. And legacy's credential selection is: per-user personal token first, else fall back to a **per-user OAuth token** (in cookies) that it refreshes using the institution's dev key. So even legacy's "institution" path still ends up as **a separate token per teacher** after each teacher authorizes once. There is no single shared token acting across all courses in legacy.

And here's the good news for you: **lawgrader's `lms_institution_configs` (migration 0219) is a faithful, cleaner port of exactly that `GROUP.canvas` model.** The plumbing you remember starting is there, it's done, and it matches legacy. So you were right that the institution-level plumbing exists. The precise name for it is an enterprise-wide **app credential (dev key)**, not an enterprise-wide **token**. It still requires each of the 30 teachers to click "authorize" once.

## The genuine fourth option you're reaching for

There *is* a true single-token model, and neither legacy nor lawgrader implements it: a BYU Canvas **admin issues one account-admin-scoped access token**, you store it once at the school level, and WriteGrader acts across all 30 courses with **zero teacher setup**. That's the real "enterprise-wide token." It would slot into the unused `schools.canvas_config`, and your existing service-role-only secret pattern (the way `lms_institution_configs` guards `client_secret`) is 90% of the plumbing it needs. Credential selection already has the right seam in `connections.ts` (the per-user-vs-institution branch).

So the full ladder, with what each costs and what's built:

| Option | Teacher setup | Institution ask | Risk you hold | Status in lawgrader |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Personal token | paste token (manual) | none | per-teacher token | ✅ built |
| 2. Institution dev key → per-teacher OAuth | one "authorize" click | issue a dev key | per-teacher tokens (revocable individually) | ✅ built (0219) = the legacy model |
| 3. **Enterprise admin token** | **nothing** | issue an admin token | **one god-token, full account** | ❌ not built (schema home exists) |
| 4. LTI 1.3 | nothing (SSO from course) | install + register a tool | no stored god-token; per-launch context | ❌ not built (only legacy's fake bridge) |

## How I'd read this for BYU

The honest tension on **option 3 (the enterprise token)**: it's the smoothest for you and the teachers (zero setup, and an admin token sees all 30 courses across all 30 separate accounts, which solves the enumeration problem from two turns ago). But it concentrates maximum risk in one stored secret, and **getting an institution's security office to hand a third party an account-admin token is often the *hardest* approval of all four**, harder than a dev key or an LTI install. That risk asymmetry is exactly why the industry standardized on LTI: institutions will install a tool but won't surrender an admin token. Your own CLAUDE.md already flags secret-sprawl as a known liability, and this would be the most valuable secret in the system.

So my read: you already built option 2, and it *is* the legacy model and Andrew is already issuing the dev key for it. That's your near-term enterprise path with the least institutional friction. Option 3 is worth offering as a configuration for schools whose IT is comfortable with it (some are, and then it's genuinely zero-setup), and it's a *small* build on the plumbing you have: store an admin token in the per-school service-role table, add one branch in `connections.ts`. Option 4 (real LTI) is the longer-term "installable institutional tool" play, and it's the one with no god-token.

The practical upshot is that you can support 2 and 3 from the **same** institution-config table with a `mode` discriminator (`oauth_dev_key` vs `admin_token`), and let each school pick based on what their IT will approve. That's probably the right enterprise design: don't pick one globally, let the institution's risk tolerance select.

message.content: Is going the LTI route hard? Is there a lot of overhead with Canvas of getting to be an authorized app?

content.text:
Short version: **building it is moderate and well-trodden; getting authorized at a single institution like BYU is low overhead, basically the same as the API dev key you already asked Andrew for.** The heavy, scary "app approval" thing you may be picturing is the public Canvas *marketplace*, and you don't need that for the enterprise motion. Let me separate the two, because they get conflated constantly.

## The build effort

LTI 1.3 sits on OIDC + OAuth2 client-credentials + JWT/JWKS. The pieces you implement:

- An **OIDC login-init endpoint** (Canvas pokes it, you redirect back with state/nonce).
- A **launch/redirect endpoint** that receives Canvas's signed `id_token` (a JWT), validates it against Canvas's public keys, and reads the claims: who the user is, their role, which course, the resource link, and the URLs for the grade/roster services.
- Your own **JWKS endpoint** plus key management (you sign assertions to fetch service tokens).
- For LTI Advantage: **NRPS** (call the memberships URL for the roster) and **AGS** (create line items, post scores). Optionally **Deep Linking** to attach a WriteGrader assignment from inside Canvas.

The conceptual learning curve is the JWT/JWKS dance and getting the nonce/state handling right (it's security-sensitive). Once you've done one launch, NRPS and AGS are straightforward calls. There's a mature Node library (`ltijs`) that handles 1.3 launch, AGS, NRPS, deep linking, and key management, which collapses most of the boilerplate.

**The one real friction for your stack:** `ltijs` is Express/Fastify-oriented and wants a persistent server plus its own datastore (Mongo by default). You're SvelteKit on Vercel serverless with Supabase. So you'd either adapt the library into serverless handlers (it fights you a bit because it wants to own routes), or implement the 1.3 flow more directly against Supabase for the nonce/registration state, which honestly isn't much code once you understand the flow. Realistic estimate for a focused pass: roughly **1 to 2 weeks** to a solid launch + roster + grade passback, depending on how hard the serverless fit fights. That's additive on top of the OAuth path you already have, not a replacement.

## The "authorized app" overhead, which is two different things

1. **Installing at one institution (BYU, and each enterprise customer).** A Canvas **admin** creates an **LTI Developer Key** in their instance (Developer Keys → + LTI Key), usually by pasting your tool's config URL, grants the AGS/NRPS scopes, sets it ON, and installs it to the account. That is it. **No Instructure-corporate involvement, no review, no marketplace.** It's the same shape of admin action as the API key Andrew is already setting up, just a different key type. So for BYU, "getting authorized" is a local form, not a gauntlet. The overhead scales per customer (each school's admin installs it), but each install is small, and **LTI Dynamic Registration** (which Canvas supports) reduces it close to "admin pastes one URL, clicks confirm."

2. **Getting listed in the public Canvas app directory (Instructure Partner / EduAppCenter).** *This* is the heavy one: partner program, security review, listing process. You only need it if you want to be discoverable in the public marketplace for broad self-serve distribution. **You do not need it to run at BYU or any individual enterprise customer.** Plenty of tools operate per-institution for years without ever being listed.

## Honest bottom line

For your situation, LTI is not a big approval mountain, it's a moderate engineering task plus a per-customer admin install that's no worse than the API key flow you're already doing. The reasons to *not* rush it: you already have the OAuth dev-key path working, Andrew is already provisioning that key, and it gets you 80% of the enterprise experience today. The reasons LTI eventually wins: zero teacher setup (SSO launch from inside the course), official grade passback via AGS instead of the 3-step file upload, no stored god-token, and the per-institution install is the thing IT security teams are *comfortable* approving (unlike the admin-token option, which is the one they balk at).

So I'd frame it as: ship on the OAuth dev key now (built, low friction), and treat LTI as the deliberate "we're now an installable institutional tool" investment, roughly a 1-to-2-week build whenever the enterprise pipeline justifies it. The marketplace listing is a separate, much later, optional decision.

message.content: So how hard would you push towards LTI versus the current plumbing I've established for prepping for Canvas institutional connection?

content.text:
Direct answer: I'd push **hard on LTI as the destination, but soft on building it now.** High conviction on direction, low urgency on timing. Ship the OAuth institutional plumbing you've built, commit to LTI as the eventual spine, and don't build it until a real signal demands it. Here's the reasoning, including the thing that makes this an easy call.

## The current plumbing is not a sunk cost, which de-risks the whole decision

The reason this isn't an agonizing fork: **LTI does not replace your REST/OAuth work, it sits alongside it.** LTI's services cover launch (SSO), roster (NRPS), and grade passback (AGS). They do *not* give you the submitted PDF files. Pulling submission content out of Canvas is a REST API call, and the LTI service token is scoped to NRPS/AGS, not arbitrary REST. So in an LTI future you will *still* need REST API access to download student submissions, which means you'll *still* want the dev-key OAuth credential you just built. The mature pattern is exactly this combo: **LTI for launch + roster + grades, REST for content.**

So the OAuth dev-key plumbing is the right near-term path *and* a permanent complement, not a bridge you'll burn. That removes the "am I wasting this work" risk that usually makes people thrash on this decision.

## Why I wouldn't pivot to LTI right now

- It works, it's tested, and Andrew is provisioning the key as we speak. Don't stall a working enterprise path for a speculative one.
- The friction it removes (each teacher does one "authorize" click) is small for a *coordinated* department. 30 MCom instructors told by their coordinator to connect Canvas will click authorize once. That friction matters at large or uncoordinated scale, not for your first pilot.
- You haven't yet validated the enterprise motion with a paying customer. Building LTI before that is optimizing a path you haven't proven anyone will walk. ~1-2 weeks of JWT/JWKS/serverless work is real cost against an unvalidated need.

## The triggers that should flip you to building LTI

Build it the moment any of these shows up, and at least one probably will:

1. **A prospect's IT says "we don't hand third parties API/dev keys, but we'll install an LTI tool."** This is common, and it's the cleanest reason. It also kills the admin-token option for that school.
2. **Onboarding drop-off** measurably traces to the per-teacher authorize step.
3. **A school requires grades as native gradebook entries** (AGS line items), not just feedback comments. Some assessment offices insist on this.
4. **You want students to SSO into the portal from inside Canvas** without separate accounts (your non-Canvas portal customers don't need this, but a Canvas school might).

Until one of those fires, the OAuth path is sufficient.

## The one thing to do now so LTI stays a drop-in

Don't let the OAuth assumption leak upward into the canon. Keep authentication behind the connection layer (the `connections.ts` seam already exists), and keep the Course/Section/Blueprint model **LMS-agnostic**, the way we designed it. A Section should know "I'm bound to Canvas course X," not "I have a per-user OAuth token." If the auth mechanism stays swappable behind the connection abstraction, adding LTI later is additive: a new connection mode, not a refactor. That costs you nothing now and keeps the door wide open.

## And the admin-token option

I'd actively steer *away* from the enterprise admin token (option 3) as a default, for the reasons last turn: it's the hardest for IT to approve and the biggest secret to hold. Offer it only to a school that specifically asks and whose IT is comfortable. Your ranked ladder is: **OAuth dev key now → LTI as the destination → admin token only on request.**

So: how hard would I push? I'd write LTI into the roadmap as the explicit enterprise integration spine, I'd preserve the abstraction seam this week, and I'd schedule the actual 1-2 week build against the first enterprise deal that needs it rather than now. That's "committed direction, deferred build," which is the posture that costs you the least while keeping the most optionality.

The LTI detour wasn't wasted, it settled the connection strategy, which was a genuinely open question. Now it's parked: ship the OAuth dev-key path, LTI later. With that closed, here's where we actually stand and what I'd build.

## Where we stand

The design is coherent and the open questions are now narrow. Decisions we've effectively settled across this conversation:

- **Canon over personal ownership.** The enterprise unit is a shared, authoritative assignment+rubric, inherited by instructors, not 30 people emailing files.
- **The Blueprint** is the keystone object: a named, versioned binding of prompt + rubric + AI guidance. The pairing is what gets standardized, versioned, and propagated, so it can never desync.
- **Partial-mirror model.** Canvas is the system of record, WriteGrader the system of engagement. The canon is LMS-agnostic; it flows into two delivery surfaces, Canvas-mirrored (teacher-only) or the native student portal (non-Canvas customers).
- **Linking stays instructor-initiated**, self-serve, per their own Canvas course. No auto-linking.
- **Connection: OAuth dev key now** (built, Andrew provisioning), LTI as the deferred destination, admin token only on request.

What's already built and reusable: schools + memberships + email-domain auto-provision + SSO scaffold; visibility enums + `is_template` + clone; `rubric_versions` with version pinning; `assignment_collaborators` and class co-teachers; the full Canvas roster/import/pushback pipeline; the institutional OAuth config. That's a lot of substrate. The gap is the **canonical layer** (Course, Blueprint, coordinator role, inheritance) and the **differentiators** (consistency, pooled billing).

## What I'd build, in order

I'd sequence this so the cheap, de-risking work comes first and each phase is independently shippable.

**Phase 1 — Department library (mostly wiring, ships fast).**
This is the legacy feature, modernized, and it's almost entirely reuse: a department-scoped library of rubrics and assignments that any instructor can browse and clone into their class. You already have `visibility='group'`, `is_template`, and clone. The build is: a "Share to department" action, a subgroup/department tag for scoping, and the library views filtered to your school/subgroup. Delivers real value (a department pools its materials) in days, and it validates that instructors will actually use shared content before you invest in the canon. It also builds the membership/scoping substrate Phase 2 needs anyway.

The honest caveat: clone-and-drift is *not* standardization. It gives starting points that diverge. That's exactly why Phase 1 is the floor, not the goal.

**Phase 2 — Course + Blueprint (the differentiator).**
This is what you actually asked for: enforced standardization with a canon that updates. New: `courses` (school + department, name, code, policy), `course_members` (coordinator/instructor/ta), `blueprints` (references a canonical rubric + pinned version + AI guidance + lock policy), `blueprint_versions` (the immutable {prompt, rubric_version, guidance} bundle), and `classes.course_id` + `term`. Instructors instantiate the Blueprint into their section, inheriting the bound prompt + rubric; the coordinator owns the canon; RLS enforces `is_course_coordinator`. This is the moment WriteGrader does something competitors who only "share files" can't.

**Phase 3 — Propagation + the term loop.**
Coordinator ships Blueprint v5; sections on v4 get a "update?" nudge; already-graded work stays pinned to the version it was graded against. Plus per-term section spawning under a Course, with the same self-serve Canvas linking. This makes the canon stay current across sections and terms without anyone rebuilding.

**Phase 4 — The enterprise-product layer.**
Cross-section consistency and norming (anchor papers, grade-spread dashboard) is the defensible-grading feature that turns "we share materials" into "we run a coordinated multi-section course," and it leans directly on your MCom validation work. Pooled credits/seats at the school level with an admin burn view is the commercial unlock (today credits are per-user). These are high value but correctly come after the canon exists.

## What I'd explicitly defer

LTI (parked). The enterprise admin token (on request only). The full `org_units` ltree hierarchy (overkill for one department, a flat subgroup is enough now). Multi-year longitudinal analytics (you dropped this). Don't let any of these expand Phase 1 or 2.

## The one decision to unblock Phase 1

Department scoping: use a lightweight **subgroup on membership** (a teacher belongs to school + "MCom") and scope the library to school/subgroup, **deferring the orphaned `org_units` hierarchy**. That's my recommendation; it's the minimum that serves BYU MCom and avoids wiring a hierarchy you don't need yet. If you'd rather light up `org_units` now for a multi-department future, that's the only reason to choose otherwise, and I'd still say not yet.

## Immediate next step

Capture all of this in `docs/enterprise-sharing-design.md` (entity model, Blueprint mechanics, partial-mirror + direction-of-truth, the two delivery surfaces, the four phases, the connection strategy with LTI marked deferred, and the abstraction-seam note so LTI stays a drop-in). That's the artifact to react to, hand Andrew, and take to the MCom coordinator. Then start Phase 1, since it's mostly wiring what already exists.

Yes, I see exactly what you mean, and it's the right instinct. Divergence should be a door that's open but clearly marked, not locked and not invisible. The way to handle it: every instantiated assignment/rubric carries its **provenance** (which Blueprint and version it came from) plus a computed **alignment state** relative to the current canon. That state is a badge. Here's how I'd build it.

## The states

It's really a three-way relationship between the instructor's working copy, the version they branched from, and the current canonical version. That yields three (and a half) states:

- **On standard** — matches the current canonical version. (Your "on program.")
- **Update available** — unmodified, but the coordinator has shipped a newer version. Faithful, just behind. One-click "adopt latest."
- **Customized** — locally edited, differs from the canon. The deliberate divergence.
- *(Customized + update available)* — the merge case, handled below.

**Tone is the whole game here.** Per what you said, deviation is allowed and sometimes wise, so the language must be informational, not punitive. "Customized," not "Out of compliance." "Adapted from Business Article v4," not "Non-conforming." That also matches the brand voice (assistant, not enforcer).

## How it's computed (cheap, reuses what exists)

The instructed section already carries `blueprint_id` + `blueprint_version_id` (the base it branched from). Add one thing: a `customized` flag that flips true on the first edit to graded substance, backed by a content hash against the base `rubric_version` snapshot you already store. Then:

- `customized = false` and `base_version == blueprint.current_version` → **On standard**
- `customized = false` and `base_version < current` → **Update available**
- `customized = true` → **Customized** (and check current for the merge case)

One important scoping rule, reusing the seam we already drew: **drift is measured on the graded core only** (rubric + graded prompt), *not* section logistics (due dates, announcements). Changing a due date is not "deviating from the standard," so it must not trip the badge. Only touching the rubric or the graded prompt counts.

## Making divergence conscious, then persistent

Two moments, because you want them to *know*:

1. **The act:** the first edit to the canonical core triggers a one-time acknowledgment. "This is your department's standard rubric. Editing it customizes your section's copy, which will show as Customized to you and your coordinator. Continue?" That turns drift from an accident into a decision.
2. **The persistent signal:** after that, a badge + provenance line rides with the artifact everywhere it appears, the builder, the grade surface, the class list: *"Customized · adapted from MCom 320 Business Article v4."* Click it for a **diff view** showing exactly what they changed versus the canon (criteria added, weights moved, descriptors rewritten), plus actions: **Reset to standard** (discard local changes) and **See the standard**. Divergence is never a one-way door, the base pointer is retained so they can always return.

## The coordinator's side (the real payoff)

The badge is most valuable inverted. The coordinator's Course view rolls up all 30 sections: who's **on standard**, who's **behind**, who's **customized**, and what each customization is. Drift becomes visible to the person who owns the canon, not just the person who created it. That's the governance value, and it's the same data, just aggregated, so it's nearly free once the per-section state exists.

## Two interactions to get right

- **Lock policy gates whether divergence is even possible.** If a Blueprint is `locked`, the badge is always "On standard" and editing is disabled (or requires coordinator permission). If `adaptable`, the badge system above runs. So the lock decides *whether*, the badge handles *making it visible when they do*.
- **Canon advances while a section is customized** (the merge case). Don't auto-merge. Surface the choice: *"The standard moved to v5. You're on a customized v4. [See what changed in v5] · [Keep mine] · [Take v5, replace my changes]."* The win is the awareness, not an automatic reconciliation.

Net: it's a small data addition (a base-version pointer you already have, plus one `customized` flag), and the value is almost entirely in the surfacing, the badge, the provenance line, the diff, and the coordinator rollup.

Want me to fold this into the design doc as the "alignment and divergence" section, and draft the exact badge copy for the four states so the tone is nailed down?

content.text:
Good challenge, and it's the right one to make before building. Pushing on it changes the sequencing, and honestly it walks back something I overstated earlier when I called Course "the keystone." Let me give you the straight answer: **for the core enterprise value, you do not need a Course entity. The Blueprint carries almost all of it.**

Look at everything we've piled onto "the canon" and ask which actually requires a Course:

- Standardized content (Business Article = prompt + rubric + AI note) → **Blueprint**
- Inheritance into a section → **Blueprint** instantiation
- Versioning and propagation (v4 → v5) → **Blueprint versions**
- The divergence badge / on-standard-vs-customized → relative to the **Blueprint**
- Who owns and can edit the canon → an owner/editor role **on the Blueprint**

None of that needs a Course. You can ship the entire sharing-and-standardization story with Blueprints living in a department-scoped library, and never introduce a Course. So your instinct is correct: rubric + assignment + AI note + Blueprint is enough for the thing the 30 MCom instructors actually need, which is "use the department's standard package in my section."

So what does a Course, and *only* a Course, buy you? Three things, and they're all the same flavor:

1. **A named program that groups several Blueprints.** MCom 320 isn't one assignment, it's the Business Article *plus* the Memo *plus* the Recommendation Report. Without a Course, those are loose items a folder or tag ties together weakly. Course makes "MCom 320's curriculum" a real object.
2. **An anchor for the *set of sections* that exists independent of content.** This is the load-bearing one. "Show grade consistency across all 30 sections of MCom 320" needs to know which classes are the same course, including a section that hasn't set anything up yet. You can *approximate* this from "all classes that instantiated Blueprint X" (instantiations point back via `blueprint_id`), but that's derived and fragile. Course gives clean, direct membership.
3. **A home for program-level role and policy.** "Sarah coordinates MCom 320" (cascading to all its Blueprints and sections), plus program-wide rules like a mandated anonymization policy. Without Course, those become per-Blueprint assignments you repeat.

Notice the pattern: every one of those is about **coordinating and analyzing across sections**, not about sharing. Sharing is a Blueprint-and-library concern. Course is a *coordination* concern. Which means Course earns its keep exactly when you build the cross-section consistency/norming dashboards and the coordinator/admin portal you mentioned, and not a moment before. The two arrive together: the Course is the central object that admin portal is built around.

So I'd re-sequence and correct myself:

- **Blueprint is the real keystone.** Build it in Phase 2. It delivers the standardization, inheritance, versioning, and divergence badge with no Course in sight.
- **Course is a Phase 4 entity**, introduced alongside cross-section consistency and the admin/coordinator portal, when "the set of sections" needs a first-class anchor. Until then a folder/tag on Blueprints substitutes fine.
- **Keep the seam so Course is additive later:** have Blueprints carry the school/department scope, and have each instantiated section keep its `blueprint_id` back-reference. Then introducing a Course is just grouping existing Blueprints and adopting existing sections, not a refactor.

Net: you were right to question it. Course is genuinely *useful* but not *necessary* for the value you're chasing first. Build Blueprints, defer Course to the coordination/analytics layer.

# Enterprise sharing & the Canvas course lifecycle — design

> Status: design, 2026-06-26. Captures the model for departments that share
> standardized assignments + rubrics across many instructors, and how that
> canon flows through Canvas every term. Motivating case: BYU MCom 320, ~30
> instructors each teaching their own section of the same course.
>
> Companions: `docs/canvas-institutional-oauth.md` (connection plumbing),
> `docs/canvas-developer-key-request.md` (the BYU dev-key ask).

## The problem

Today every rubric, assignment, and class is owned by one user (`owner_user_id`).
That's right for a solo teacher and wrong for a department. The MCom case makes
the gap concrete:

> 30 instructors teaching MCom 320 are not 30 people who occasionally share
> files. They teach one course with one canon, in 30 sections, and the
> department wants that canon to be standard, current, and inheritable.

The legacy WriteGrader system reached for this with groups, subgroups
(departments), a shared library filtered by subgroup, signup codes, and
copy-on-use templates. We can do better than clone-and-drift: a named,
versioned canon that instructors inherit and can knowingly diverge from.

## The keystone: Blueprint (not Course)

A **Blueprint** is the first-class object that carries standardization. It is a
*named, versioned binding* of:

- a canonical assignment prompt (graded substance, not logistics),
- a specific rubric (referenced from the rubric library, pinned to a version),
- the shared AI grading guidance (`ai_setup`).

Assignments and rubrics stay independent, reusable citizens. The Blueprint is
the third citizen that says "these two, together, with this guidance, are how we
teach this." MCom's Business Article is one Blueprint.

**Why the binding is its own object:** the thing a coordinator maintains over
time is the *pairing*, and they want one version timeline for it, not two they
must keep in sync. A Blueprint version is an immutable snapshot of
`{ prompt, rubric_version_id, ai_setup }`. Pinning a section to a Blueprint
version transitively pins the right prompt *and* the right rubric, so the pairing
can never desync. An instructor can't accidentally run this year's prompt against
last year's rubric.

### What the Blueprint delivers (no Course required)

- Standardized content (the canonical package).
- Inheritance: a section instantiates a Blueprint version.
- Versioning + propagation: v4 → v5, pushed to sections, already-graded work
  stays pinned to the version it was graded against.
- Divergence tracking (the badge, below).
- Ownership / edit authority (a coordinator/owner on the Blueprint).

### Inheritance splits along a seam

When an instructor sets up a Blueprint in their section, inheritance covers the
**graded substance** (prompt, rubric, AI guidance) and never the **section
logistics** (due date, availability window, announcements). Logistics are always
section-local and never count as divergence. This seam is reused throughout
(e.g. drift detection ignores logistics).

### Lock / adapt policy (per Blueprint)

- `locked` — instructors use the canon as-is; editing the graded core is
  disabled (or requires coordinator permission). Default for high-stakes shared
  courses.
- `adaptable` — instructors may diverge; the alignment badge tracks state.

The lock policy decides *whether* divergence is possible; the badge system makes
it *visible* when it happens.

## Alignment and divergence

Divergence is an open door, clearly marked, never invisible. Every instantiated
artifact carries its **provenance** (which Blueprint + base version) plus a
computed **alignment state** relative to the current canon.

State is a three-way relationship between the instructor's working copy, the
version they branched from (`base_version`), and the Blueprint's current version:

| State | Meaning | Action offered |
|---|---|---|
| **On standard** | matches current canonical version | none |
| **Update available** | unmodified but a newer version exists | adopt latest (one click) |
| **Customized** | locally edited, differs from canon | see diff · reset to standard |
| **Customized + update available** | edited *and* canon advanced | see what changed · keep mine · take new (replace) |

**Computation is cheap:** the section already carries `blueprint_id` +
`blueprint_version_id` (the base). Add a `customized` flag that flips true on the
first edit to graded substance, backed by a content hash against the base
`rubric_version` snapshot we already store. Drift is measured on the graded core
only; changing a due date never trips the badge.

**Making divergence conscious, then persistent:**

1. *The act* — the first edit to the canonical core triggers a one-time
   acknowledgment: "This is your department's standard rubric. Editing customizes
   your section's copy, which will show as Customized to you and your
   coordinator. Continue?" Turns drift from accident into decision.
2. *The persistent signal* — a badge + provenance line rides with the artifact
   everywhere (builder, grade surface, class list): "Customized · adapted from
   MCom 320 Business Article v4." Click for a diff vs the canon and actions
   (reset to standard, see the standard). The base pointer is always retained, so
   returning is never a one-way door.

**Tone is informational, not punitive.** "Customized," not "out of compliance."
Divergence is allowed and sometimes wise. (Matches brand voice: assistant, not
enforcer.)

**Coordinator rollup (the payoff):** the same per-section state, aggregated, lets
a coordinator see across all sections who is on standard, behind, or customized,
and exactly what each customization is. Drift becomes visible to the owner of the
canon. Nearly free once per-section state exists.

## Course — the coordination anchor (deferred)

A **Course** (e.g. "MCom 320") is a named program that groups several Blueprints
and anchors the set of sections. It is genuinely useful but **not necessary** for
the core sharing/standardization value, which lives entirely on the Blueprint.

Course earns its keep only when you need:

1. to group several Blueprints as a named program (Business Article + Memo + …),
2. an anchor for *the set of sections* that exists independent of content
   (needed for cross-section consistency/norming, roster rollup, program-level
   coordinator scope),
3. a home for program-level role and policy (a coordinator who cascades to all
   the program's Blueprints and sections; a mandated anonymization policy).

All three are *coordination/analytics* concerns, not *sharing* concerns. So
Course arrives with the cross-section consistency dashboards and the
coordinator/admin portal (Phase 4), not before. Until then a folder/tag on
Blueprints substitutes.

**Keep the seam so Course is additive later:** Blueprints carry the
school/department scope, and each instantiated section keeps its `blueprint_id`
back-reference. Introducing a Course is then just grouping existing Blueprints and
adopting existing sections, not a refactor.

## Partial mirror: WriteGrader over Canvas

For customers on Canvas, **Canvas is the system of record; WriteGrader is the
system of engagement.** WriteGrader mirrors only the courses an instructor opts
in, only their rosters, only the assignments they want graded. "Partial" is
load-bearing: it's the privacy/FERPA story (we reflect what you point us at, we
don't ingest the institution) and the commercial boundary (mirror scope = seat
scope).

A coherent mirror needs a stated direction of truth per entity:

| Entity | System of record | WriteGrader does | Conflict rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roster / enrollment | Canvas | reflect (re-pull) | never write back; Canvas wins |
| Submissions | Canvas | pull copies | Canvas wins |
| Rubric / feedback / AI grade | WriteGrader | author | WriteGrader wins (work product) |
| Official gradebook grade | Canvas | propose via pushback | don't clobber a teacher's manual override |
| Assignment metadata | contested | create-from-Blueprint or link existing | needs an explicit rule per field |

**Staleness is first-class, not an edge case.** The concrete pain is drop/add
week: a student enrolls in Canvas after the link, submits, and we've never heard
of them. Surface "roster last synced N days ago — refresh?" using the
`canvas_students.last_synced_at` heartbeat we already have.

### Two delivery surfaces, one canon

The canon (Course/Blueprint) is **LMS-agnostic**. A section is either:

- **Canvas-mirrored** — students live in Canvas; teacher-only in WriteGrader;
  feedback pushed back. (Customers with Canvas.)
- **Native portal** — students use the WriteGrader student portal. (Customers
  without Canvas.)

Same Blueprint flows into both. One product, two collection surfaces.

## Canvas course lifecycle (per term)

Empirical reality at BYU MCom: **30 instructors, 30 separate Canvas courses, each
in their own account**, no shared parent course. So a WriteGrader Course is a
purely WriteGrader-side grouping over 30 unrelated Canvas course ids. There is no
single Canvas place to enumerate them from — which is why linking is, and should
be, instructor-initiated.

**Linking is self-serve and never automatic.** A mirror reflects what you point at
it. The instructor points WriteGrader at their Canvas course (the existing
`linkCanvasCourse` action sets `classes.canvas_course_id` + `lms_connection_id`).
We never auto-create or auto-link. The canon is *offered* into the mirrored
section, not forced.

**Durable spine vs. ephemeral instances.** Canvas mints a new course id each term
even for the same `course_code`. So:

- Course + Blueprint = durable, live for years.
- Section (LawGrader class) + Canvas course id = ephemeral, one per
  instructor-per-term.

Term rollover is therefore "spawn a new section under the Course," not "relink an
old class to a new course." Last term's section stays as history. (This dissolves
the rollover gap in the current 1:1 sticky link, and only needs `classes.course_id`
+ `term` once Course exists.)

Durable across terms: the Course, the Blueprint history, and each instructor's
`lms_connections` row (connect Canvas once). Refreshes each term: the
section↔Canvas mapping, the roster, the Canvas assignment ids.

## LMS connection strategy

Four ways to authenticate to Canvas, by who does the setup:

| Option | Teacher setup | Institution ask | Risk held | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Personal token | paste token | none | per-teacher token | built (`scope='personal_api_token'`) |
| 2. Institution OAuth dev key → per-teacher OAuth | one "authorize" click | issue a dev key | per-teacher tokens (individually revocable) | **built** (0219 `lms_institution_configs` + `scope='oauth'`) — matches legacy `GROUP.canvas` |
| 3. Enterprise admin token | nothing | issue an account-admin token | one god-token, full account | not built (home: unused `schools.canvas_config`) |
| 4. LTI 1.3 | nothing (SSO from course) | install + register a tool | no stored god-token; per-launch context | not built (legacy has only a deprecated fake bridge) |

**Decision:**

- **Ship option 2 now.** It's built, it's the legacy model, and BYU is already
  issuing the dev key. Note: it still mints a *per-teacher* token (each clicks
  "authorize" once); the "enterprise-wide" part is the *app credential*, not the
  token.
- **Option 4 (LTI) is the destination, deferred.** Build it (~1–2 weeks,
  additive) when a real signal demands it: a prospect's IT won't issue API keys
  but will install an LTI tool; measured onboarding drop-off on the authorize
  step; a school requires native gradebook (AGS) entries; students need SSO from
  inside Canvas. LTI does *not* replace REST — you still need REST for submission
  file content, so option 2's plumbing is a permanent complement, not a sunk cost.
  Per-institution LTI install is a local admin action (like the dev key); the
  public marketplace listing is separate, heavy, and not needed for the
  enterprise motion.
- **Option 3 (admin token) on request only.** Smoothest for teachers (zero
  setup), but the hardest for IT to approve and the biggest secret to hold. Offer
  it to a school whose IT specifically wants it. Small build on existing
  service-role-secret plumbing (store a token in the per-school config, add one
  branch in `connections.ts`).

**Near-term action to keep LTI a drop-in:** keep authentication behind the
connection layer (`connections.ts` seam) and keep the Course/Blueprint canon
LMS-agnostic. A Section knows "I'm bound to Canvas course X," not "I hold a
per-user OAuth token." Then adding LTI later is a new connection mode, not a
refactor.

## Build phases

Cheap, de-risking work first; each phase independently shippable.

**Phase 1 — Department library (mostly wiring).**
Reuse `visibility='group'`, `is_template`, clone. Add a "share to department"
action, a subgroup/department tag for scoping, and library views filtered to the
viewer's school/subgroup. Delivers a department pool of rubrics + assignments any
instructor can clone. Validates that instructors use shared content, and builds
the membership/scoping substrate later phases need. (Honest caveat:
clone-and-drift is not standardization — this is the floor, not the goal.)

**Phase 2 — Blueprint + inheritance + divergence (the differentiator).**
New: `blueprints` (course-or-department scope, name, references a canonical
rubric + pinned version + `ai_setup` + lock policy) and `blueprint_versions`
(immutable `{ prompt, rubric_version_id, ai_setup }` bundle). Instantiate a
Blueprint into a section, inheriting the bound prompt + rubric. Add the alignment
badge + provenance + diff + reset. This is the standardization story.

**Phase 3 — Propagation + term loop.**
Coordinator ships v5; sections on v4 get an "update?" nudge; graded work stays
pinned. Per-term section spawning, still self-serve linking to each teacher's
Canvas course.

**Phase 4 — Coordination layer.**
Introduce **Course** (`courses`, `course_members` with coordinator/instructor/ta,
`classes.course_id` + `term`). Build cross-section consistency / norming (anchor
papers, grade-spread dashboard — leans on the MCom validation work). Build the
coordinator/admin portal (Course is its central object). Pooled credits/seats at
the school level with an admin burn view (today credits are per-user).

## Deferred / out of scope (for now)

- LTI (parked; the destination, not now).
- Enterprise admin token as a default (on request only).
- The full `org_units` ltree hierarchy (a flat subgroup is enough for one
  department; light it up only for a multi-department future).
- Multi-year longitudinal student analytics (dropped — email-as-join-key is fine).

## Open questions

- **Department model:** use a lightweight `memberships.subgroup` and scope the
  library to school/subgroup, **deferring `org_units`**. (Recommended.) Only
  choose otherwise to light up a multi-department hierarchy now.
- **Pooled billing design:** a credit ledger owned by the org rather than the
  user is a real schema change and the biggest commercial unlock; scoped in
  Phase 4, design TBD.
- **UI manifestation + admin portal:** how all of this surfaces in the UI is not
  yet designed; a coordinator/admin portal is expected and arrives with Phase 4.

## Existing primitives to build on

- Identity: `schools`, `memberships(role, subgroup)`, `school_email_domains`
  (email-domain auto-provision), SSO scaffold.
- Sharing: `visibility` enum (private/group/public), `is_template` +
  `template_source_id` + clone, `assignment_collaborators`, class `shared_with`,
  `join_code`.
- Versioning: `rubric_versions` (immutable snapshots) + `current_rubric_version_id`
  pinning.
- Canvas: `lms_connections`, `lms_institution_configs`, `canvas_resource_links`,
  `canvas_students`, the import/roster/pushback pipeline, `connections.ts`
  credential seam.
- Orphaned, do not wire yet: `org_units` / `org_unit_members`,
  `schools.canvas_config`, `schools.lti_client_id`.

| **On standard** | matches current canonical version | none |
| **Update available** | unmodified but a newer version exists | adopt latest (one click) |
| **Customized** | locally edited, differs from canon | see diff · reset to standard |
| **Customized + update available** | edited *and* canon advanced | see what changed · keep mine · take new (replace) |

**Computation is cheap:** the section already carries `blueprint_id` +
`blueprint_version_id` (the base). Add a `customized` flag that flips true on the
first edit to graded substance, backed by a content hash against the base
`rubric_version` snapshot we already store. Drift is measured on the graded core
only; changing a due date never trips the badge.

**Making divergence conscious, then persistent:**

1. *The act* — the first edit to the canonical core triggers a one-time
   acknowledgment: "This is your department's standard rubric. Editing customizes
   your section's copy, which will show as Customized to you and your
   coordinator. Continue?" Turns drift from accident into decision.
2. *The persistent signal* — a badge + provenance line rides with the artifact
   everywhere (builder, grade surface, class list): "Customized · adapted from
   MCom 320 Business Article v4." Click for a diff vs the canon and actions
   (reset to standard, see the standard). The base pointer is always retained, so
   returning is never a one-way door.

**Tone is informational, not punitive.** "Customized," not "out of compliance."
Divergence is allowed and sometimes wise. (Matches brand voice: assistant, not
enforcer.)

**Coordinator rollup (the payoff):** the same per-section state, aggregated, lets
a coordinator see across all sections who is on standard, behind, or customized,
and exactly what each customization is. Drift becomes visible to the owner of the
canon. Nearly free once per-section state exists.

## Course — the coordination anchor (deferred)

A **Course** (e.g. "MCom 320") is a named program that groups several Blueprints
and anchors the set of sections. It is genuinely useful but **not necessary** for
the core sharing/standardization value, which lives entirely on the Blueprint.

Course earns its keep only when you need:

1. to group several Blueprints as a named program (Business Article + Memo + …),
2. an anchor for *the set of sections* that exists independent of content
   (needed for cross-section consistency/norming, roster rollup, program-level
   coordinator scope),
3. a home for program-level role and policy (a coordinator who cascades to all
   the program's Blueprints and sections; a mandated anonymization policy).

All three are *coordination/analytics* concerns, not *sharing* concerns. So
Course arrives with the cross-section consistency dashboards and the
coordinator/admin portal (Phase 4), not before. Until then a folder/tag on
Blueprints substitutes.

**Keep the seam so Course is additive later:** Blueprints carry the
school/department scope, and each instantiated section keeps its `blueprint_id`
back-reference. Introducing a Course is then just grouping existing Blueprints and
adopting existing sections, not a refactor.

## Partial mirror: WriteGrader over Canvas

For customers on Canvas, **Canvas is the system of record; WriteGrader is the
system of engagement.** WriteGrader mirrors only the courses an instructor opts
in, only their rosters, only the assignments they want graded. "Partial" is
load-bearing: it's the privacy/FERPA story (we reflect what you point us at, we
don't ingest the institution) and the commercial boundary (mirror scope = seat
scope).

A coherent mirror needs a stated direction of truth per entity:

| Entity | System of record | WriteGrader does | Conflict rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roster / enrollment | Canvas | reflect (re-pull) | never write back; Canvas wins |
| Submissions | Canvas | pull copies | Canvas wins |
| Rubric / feedback / AI grade | WriteGrader | author | WriteGrader wins (work product) |
| Official gradebook grade | Canvas | propose via pushback | don't clobber a teacher's manual override |
| Assignment metadata | contested | create-from-Blueprint or link existing | needs an explicit rule per field |

**Staleness is first-class, not an edge case.** The concrete pain is drop/add
week: a student enrolls in Canvas after the link, submits, and we've never heard
of them. Surface "roster last synced N days ago — refresh?" using the
`canvas_students.last_synced_at` heartbeat we already have.

### Two delivery surfaces, one canon

The canon (Course/Blueprint) is **LMS-agnostic**. A section is either:

- **Canvas-mirrored** — students live in Canvas; teacher-only in WriteGrader;
  feedback pushed back. (Customers with Canvas.)
- **Native portal** — students use the WriteGrader student portal. (Customers
  without Canvas.)

Same Blueprint flows into both. One product, two collection surfaces.

## Canvas course lifecycle (per term)

Empirical reality at BYU MCom: **30 instructors, 30 separate Canvas courses, each
in their own account**, no shared parent course. So a WriteGrader Course is a
purely WriteGrader-side grouping over 30 unrelated Canvas course ids. There is no
single Canvas place to enumerate them from — which is why linking is, and should
be, instructor-initiated.

**Linking is self-serve and never automatic.** A mirror reflects what you point at
it. The instructor points WriteGrader at their Canvas course (the existing
`linkCanvasCourse` action sets `classes.canvas_course_id` + `lms_connection_id`).
We never auto-create or auto-link. The canon is *offered* into the mirrored
section, not forced.

**Durable spine vs. ephemeral instances.** Canvas mints a new course id each term
even for the same `course_code`. So:

- Course + Blueprint = durable, live for years.
- Section (LawGrader class) + Canvas course id = ephemeral, one per
  instructor-per-term.

Term rollover is therefore "spawn a new section under the Course," not "relink an
old class to a new course." Last term's section stays as history. (This dissolves
the rollover gap in the current 1:1 sticky link, and only needs `classes.course_id`
+ `term` once Course exists.)

Durable across terms: the Course, the Blueprint history, and each instructor's
`lms_connections` row (connect Canvas once). Refreshes each term: the
section↔Canvas mapping, the roster, the Canvas assignment ids.

## LMS connection strategy

Four ways to authenticate to Canvas, by who does the setup:

| Option | Teacher setup | Institution ask | Risk held | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Personal token | paste token | none | per-teacher token | built (`scope='personal_api_token'`) |
| 2. Institution OAuth dev key → per-teacher OAuth | one "authorize" click | issue a dev key | per-teacher tokens (individually revocable) | **built** (0219 `lms_institution_configs` + `scope='oauth'`) — matches legacy `GROUP.canvas` |
| 3. Enterprise admin token | nothing | issue an account-admin token | one god-token, full account | not built (home: unused `schools.canvas_config`) |
| 4. LTI 1.3 | nothing (SSO from course) | install + register a tool | no stored god-token; per-launch context | not built (legacy has only a deprecated fake bridge) |

**Decision:**

- **Ship option 2 now.** It's built, it's the legacy model, and BYU is already
  issuing the dev key. Note: it still mints a *per-teacher* token (each clicks
  "authorize" once); the "enterprise-wide" part is the *app credential*, not the
  token.
- **Option 4 (LTI) is the destination, deferred.** Build it (~1–2 weeks,
  additive) when a real signal demands it: a prospect's IT won't issue API keys
  but will install an LTI tool; measured onboarding drop-off on the authorize
  step; a school requires native gradebook (AGS) entries; students need SSO from
  inside Canvas. LTI does *not* replace REST — you still need REST for submission
  file content, so option 2's plumbing is a permanent complement, not a sunk cost.
  Per-institution LTI install is a local admin action (like the dev key); the
  public marketplace listing is separate, heavy, and not needed for the
  enterprise motion.
- **Option 3 (admin token) on request only.** Smoothest for teachers (zero
  setup), but the hardest for IT to approve and the biggest secret to hold. Offer
  it to a school whose IT specifically wants it. Small build on existing
  service-role-secret plumbing (store a token in the per-school config, add one
  branch in `connections.ts`).

**Near-term action to keep LTI a drop-in:** keep authentication behind the
connection layer (`connections.ts` seam) and keep the Course/Blueprint canon
LMS-agnostic. A Section knows "I'm bound to Canvas course X," not "I hold a
per-user OAuth token." Then adding LTI later is a new connection mode, not a
refactor.

## Build phases

Cheap, de-risking work first; each phase independently shippable.

**Phase 1 — Department library (mostly wiring).**
Reuse `visibility='group'`, `is_template`, clone. Add a "share to department"
action, a subgroup/department tag for scoping, and library views filtered to the
viewer's school/subgroup. Delivers a department pool of rubrics + assignments any
instructor can clone. Validates that instructors use shared content, and builds
the membership/scoping substrate later phases need. (Honest caveat:
clone-and-drift is not standardization — this is the floor, not the goal.)

**Phase 2 — Blueprint + inheritance + divergence (the differentiator).**
New: `blueprints` (course-or-department scope, name, references a canonical
rubric + pinned version + `ai_setup` + lock policy) and `blueprint_versions`
(immutable `{ prompt, rubric_version_id, ai_setup }` bundle). Instantiate a
Blueprint into a section, inheriting the bound prompt + rubric. Add the alignment
badge + provenance + diff + reset. This is the standardization story.

**Phase 3 — Propagation + term loop.**
Coordinator ships v5; sections on v4 get an "update?" nudge; graded work stays
pinned. Per-term section spawning, still self-serve linking to each teacher's
Canvas course.

**Phase 4 — Coordination layer.**
Introduce **Course** (`courses`, `course_members` with coordinator/instructor/ta,
`classes.course_id` + `term`). Build cross-section consistency / norming (anchor
papers, grade-spread dashboard — leans on the MCom validation work). Build the
coordinator/admin portal (Course is its central object). Pooled credits/seats at
the school level with an admin burn view (today credits are per-user).

## Deferred / out of scope (for now)

- LTI (parked; the destination, not now).
- Enterprise admin token as a default (on request only).
- The full `org_units` ltree hierarchy (a flat subgroup is enough for one
  department; light it up only for a multi-department future).
- Multi-year longitudinal student analytics (dropped — email-as-join-key is fine).

## Open questions

- **Department model:** use a lightweight `memberships.subgroup` and scope the
  library to school/subgroup, **deferring `org_units`**. (Recommended.) Only
  choose otherwise to light up a multi-department hierarchy now.
- **Pooled billing design:** a credit ledger owned by the org rather than the
  user is a real schema change and the biggest commercial unlock; scoped in
  Phase 4, design TBD.
- **UI manifestation + admin portal:** how all of this surfaces in the UI is not
  yet designed; a coordinator/admin portal is expected and arrives with Phase 4.

## Existing primitives to build on

- Identity: `schools`, `memberships(role, subgroup)`, `school_email_domains`
  (email-domain auto-provision), SSO scaffold.
- Sharing: `visibility` enum (private/group/public), `is_template` +
  `template_source_id` + clone, `assignment_collaborators`, class `shared_with`,
  `join_code`.
- Versioning: `rubric_versions` (immutable snapshots) + `current_rubric_version_id`
  pinning.
- Canvas: `lms_connections`, `lms_institution_configs`, `canvas_resource_links`,
  `canvas_students`, the import/roster/pushback pipeline, `connections.ts`
  credential seam.
- Orphaned, do not wire yet: `org_units` / `org_unit_members`,
  `schools.canvas_config`, `schools.lti_client_id`.

content.text:
Good question to pause on, and my answer is a firm **mock the novel affordances now, discover the rest while building** — not a full mock suite, not pure build-and-figure-it-out. Here's the reasoning, then I'll make it concrete.

The split is about novelty. Most of Phase 1 (a department library you browse and clone) is a variation on screens you already have; you'll get those right while building, and mocking them is low-yield. But three affordances in this design are genuinely *new* interaction patterns with no precedent in the app, and those are exactly the ones that get churned if you build them blind:

1. **The alignment/divergence system** — the badge, the provenance line, the three states in context. This is the signature new thing and the one you said you can't yet picture.
2. **The customize-acknowledgment moment** — the "you're departing from the standard" dialog.
3. **The Blueprint-into-section instantiation** — "set up the Business Article in your section" inheriting prompt + rubric.

These are worth seeing before building because they're conceptual, they're load-bearing, and they constrain what data the screens expose. The coordinator rollup is also novel but it's Phase 4, so it can wait. You're design-first, so a couple of high-fidelity anchors now will save a build-churn cycle later.

Rather than just assert that, let me anchor it. I'll pull your actual Manuscript++ tokens so the mock reads as real WriteGrader, then build the signature screen (the alignment/divergence affordance in context) so you have something concrete to react to.

content.content: 1 # LawGrader brand 2 3 The single source of truth for how LawGrader looks and sounds. Mechanical token values live in [`docs/design-tokens.md`](./docs/design-tokens.md); the _why_ and the non-color decisions (wordmark, voice, assets) live here. When the two disagree, this file and `src/app.css` win and the loser gets fixed. 4 5 The palette is internally nicknamed **"Manuscript++."** The brief: a legal-writing tool should feel like a well-made legal _document_, warm paper, iron-gall ink, a glint of brass, not like generic SaaS. Professional without being boring. 6 7 --- 8 9 ## 1. The three moves 10 11 1. **Warm rag-paper base.** Off-white, faintly warm neutrals (`canvas` `#fdfcf9`). Never cool gray, never pure `#fff` as the page. 12 2. **Iron-gall indigo brand.** `brand-600` `#4855a8` → `brand-900` `#1f2860`. The blue of the ink early legal documents were written in. This is the _interactive_ color (buttons, links, focus). 13 3. **Brass accent.** `accent-600` `#b9883a`. One warm, tarnished antique-gold note: scales, gavel band, gilt on a leather spine. Decorative emphasis only, used sparingly. 14 15 A serif display face over a sans body is the fourth, load-bearing move: the serif/sans split is most of what makes the product read as _legal manuscript_. **Brand-forward surfaces** (the wordmark and the marketing/landing headings) are set in **Newsreader** (the brand face). **In-app content headings** use **Georgia**, a system serif — familiar to the audience, no webfont, and it prints cleanly to PDF. See `docs/design-tokens.md` → Type. 16 17 Direction was chosen from `design-mocks/palette-directions.html` (variant **A · iron-gall indigo + brass**). That file also holds the rejected oxblood and library-green explorations for the record. 18 19 --- 20 21 ## 2. Color 22 23 Full token tables, hex values, and contrast pairings: **[`docs/design-tokens.md`](./docs/design-tokens.md)**. The one rule worth repeating here: 24 25 > **Brand ≠ accent.** `brand-600` is the interactive blue (buttons, links, focus). Brass is decorative emphasis (the wordmark "Grader," a marketing CTA on a dark band, "released/done" flourishes). A brass button is never the default action. 26 27 --- 28 29 ## 3. The wordmark 30 31 **LawGrader**, set in Newsreader (the brand serif), weight 600, tight tracking (`-0.015em`). content.text:
That mapping holds, and the better news is your surface already has the scaffolding for most of it. Two of the three affordances are *evolutions of patterns you already ship*, not new inventions. Here's the grounded version.

## Your gateway is already a real thing: `RubricSlot`'s mode machine

The "gateway landing page that prompts them to start from a template" is `RubricSlot` (`src/lib/components/assignment-builder/RubricSlot.svelte`), which runs a mode machine: `attached / change-source / browse-library / build`. The non-attached modes (browse-library, the launch gate) are exactly the gateway you're describing. So **adoption lives here**, and the Panel 3 "adopt a Blueprint" card isn't a new screen, it's a new category ("Department standards") in the existing browse-library mode, sitting next to the template/library browse you already have.

## The builder keeps the persistent affordances, and you already have weak versions of both

**Provenance line, you already have it.** `RubricSlot` has `sourceMeta` (lines ~209-250): it maps a `rubricSource` enum (`ai_generate / ai_suggest / library / blank / upload`) to an icon + label like "Picked from your library." That *is* a provenance line. The Blueprint version is one more source value plus a version: add `standard` → "From the MCom 320 standard · v4," reusing the exact icon+label pattern. Not net-new UI.

**The badge belongs in the `RubricChatBuilder` breadcrumb header.** That header (`RubricChatBuilder.svelte`, ~lines 1157-1220) already holds: back button · editable rubric-name input · save-status chip · Done. The alignment badge slots in **right after the name input (~line 1179)**, as a chip matching `SaveStatusChip`'s vocabulary (it already does Spinner/Check/Alert + label), so "On standard / Update available / Customized" reads as a sibling of "Saved." That's the persistent signal you wanted in the builder.

**The first-edit acknowledgment is an upgrade of a banner you already show.** `RubricSlot` lines ~535-541 already render an amber banner, "Editing creates a copy of this rubric for this assignment on save," gated on `isShared && mode === "attached"`, and it already auto-forks on edit (the `reuseCount` / `saveRubricAssignmentOnly` path). So you already intercept "first edit to a shared rubric." The Blueprint acknowledgment is the same seam (`submitNow()` at ~line 322, ultimately `persistRubric`), with richer semantics: the gate generalizes from "is this reused" to "is this attached to a department standard," and the message gains the coordinator-visibility line.

## The one distinction to keep straight

Your *current* "shared rubric" means one teacher reusing a rubric across their own assignments, where forking exists to avoid clobbering. The *new* "department standard" means a coordinator's canon shared across teachers, where forking means divergence-from-standard. **Same fork mechanic, different meaning.** Reuse the plumbing (the auto-fork, the `customized` flag can ride on the same path), but the messaging and the coordinator-rollup layer are the genuinely new part. Don't let the existing "creates a copy for this assignment" copy stand in for "you're departing from the department standard", they're different stories.

## What does *not* live only on the rubric builder

Because a Blueprint binds prompt + rubric + AI guidance, the same badge + provenance has to also appear on the **assignment build page header** (the prompt is canon too) and the **grade surface** (so a grader sees which standard they're applying). So build the badge + provenance as a small shared component, and mount it in three headers. The first-edit acknowledgment and diff/reset, though, are genuinely builder-local for the rubric side.

So your instinct was right on both counts: adoption at the `RubricSlot` gateway, persistent signals in the `RubricChatBuilder` header, and most of it is extending `sourceMeta`, `SaveStatusChip`, and the existing shared-rubric fork banner rather than starting fresh.

Want me to redo the mock against your *actual* builder header layout (back · name · **badge** · save-status · Done) and the `RubricSlot` browse-library gateway, so you're looking at the affordances in your real chrome instead of a generic card? That's the version worth putting in front of yourself before any code.

Sent. This version sits in your actual builder chrome. Here's how each panel maps to the real code, so it's an implementation sketch, not just a picture:

**A — the badge + provenance strip, three states.** The badge drops into the `RubricChatBuilder` breadcrumb header (`~line 1179`, right after the rubric-name input, before the save chip), styled as a sibling of your existing save-status chip. The provenance line rides a thin strip directly under the header, the same slot your standalone builder already uses for the blast-radius strip. The strip is where the stateful actions live: nothing when on standard, "See what changed / Adopt v5" when behind, "See diff / Reset to standard" when customized. Keeps the header row clean.

**B — in situ.** Same header + strip above your real `canvas-warm` toolbar and the `# · Criterion · Mode · Scale · Weight · AI` grid. The two off-standard weights show in `warning` color with an inline "edited" tag, so divergence is legible on the grid itself, reusing your `sourceMeta` provenance vocabulary rather than inventing one.

**C — the gateway.** This is `RubricSlot`'s `browse-library` mode. The new "Department standards · MCom 320" row sits above your existing cold-start doors (Upload / Template / Draft with AI). "Use in my section" is the adopt action that instantiates the Blueprint; the badge from panel A then rides into the builder. Adoption happens here, not in the builder, exactly your instinct.

**D — first edit.** This is the upgrade of the amber "Editing creates a copy of this rubric for this assignment" banner you already show (`RubricSlot ~535-541`), hooked at the same `submitNow()` / `persistRubric` seam. Same fork mechanic you have today; the new part is the department-standard framing and the coordinator-visibility line.

So the honest takeaway: on your real surface, this is mostly **extending three things you already ship**, the `sourceMeta` provenance, the `SaveStatusChip` chip vocabulary, and the shared-rubric fork banner, plus one new category in the `RubricSlot` gateway. The only genuinely net-new surfaces are the diff view and (later) the coordinator rollup.

Want me to fold these two mocks into the design doc as a short "UI grounding" section with the anchor points (file + line) called out, so the doc carries the where-it-attaches detail alongside the model? Both mock files stay in `.mockups/` (gitignored); I'd reference them, not commit them.
